body_html:
The Northern Hydro-Meteorological Station, in a page on the Vietnam Hydro-Meteorological Administration site, expected Hanoi to be affected by 11-15 heat spells between 7 April 2026 and September 2026, with June possibly reaching 39-41 degrees C. For anyone planning a scooter ride in Hanoi's summer heat, this article reports what that outlook, the service's own heat definitions and heat-related pages from WHO, Smartraveller, the CDC (United States), the UK Highway Code and Ontario's Motorcycle Handbook say about timing, hydration and felt heat. It also lists what none of them covers.

How Vietnam's forecasters define heat

The Vietnam Hydro-Meteorological Administration's page on concepts related to heat (Các khái niệm liên quan đến nắng nóng, dated 8 May 2025) sorts days by the day's maximum temperature (Tx):

LevelDay's maximum temperature (Tx)
Heat (nắng nóng)35 degrees C or more, below 37
Severe heat (nắng nóng gay gắt)37 degrees C or more, below 39
Exceptionally severe heat (nắng nóng đặc biệt gay gắt)39 degrees C or more

The page adds that in a forecast region such as the Northern delta, a day when at least half of the stations reach 35 degrees counts as widespread heat, and widespread heat on two or more consecutive days is a heat spell (đợt nắng nóng). A day counts as widespread severe heat when at least two-thirds of stations reach 35 degrees and at least half reach 37.

What the outlook says about Hanoi's summer

The Hanoi page of 7 April 2026 gives this seasonal estimate:

PeriodHeat spells for HanoiDetail given
April to June3-5, each 2 days or moreJune may bring severe and exceptionally severe heat, with absolute maximums of 39-41 degrees C
July to September8-10 (heat and severe heat)Concentrated mainly in July and the first half of August
April to September11-15 in totalEstimate made on 7 April 2026

This is a forecast made in April. No page read here reports what June or July 2026 actually brought.

The hours when heat concentrates

For 7 and 8 April 2026 the same Hanoi page forecast widespread heat and says heat above 35 degrees is concentrated between 12:00 and 16:00 each day. A National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting (NCHMF) bulletin, whose page shows no year, gives a hot-time window of 11-16 (column headed hours; it reads as 11:00 to 16:00) for the North except Điện Biên, Lai Châu and Sơn La on 1 September and a lowest relative humidity of 45-50%. Smartraveller advises travellers in extreme heat to plan days to avoid being outside during the hottest part of the day, to take rests and to stay in shade. WHO's tips suggest breaks in shaded or air-conditioned spaces when possible. These windows belong to particular days and are not a riding timetable; no page says which hours suit a scooter ride. For route ideas, see Motorbike Rental Hanoi: Best Day Trips Around the City.

Forecast numbers, humidity and felt heat

Two Vietnamese pages warn that forecast temperatures can differ from what is felt outdoors. The 7 April 2026 Hanoi page gives 2-4 degrees C or more, depending on surfaces such as concrete, asphalt and glass; the NCHMF bulletin gives 1-3 degrees or more, naming concrete and asphalt. The pages do not reconcile the two ranges.

The Vietnamese levels above use the day's maximum temperature. The NIOSH bulletin from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes the heat index differently: a measure of how hot it feels when relative humidity is taken into account along with the actual air temperature. It adds that heat index values were devised for shady, light-wind conditions, so full sunshine can raise them by up to 15°F (the page uses Fahrenheit). Smartraveller says high humidity can make it seem hotter than it is and makes it harder for the body to cool itself through sweating. The CDC page, written for outdoor workers, calls the heat index a screening tool: as it rises, more water and rest breaks may become necessary, and in extreme-risk conditions it may be necessary to reschedule non-essential work. No page gives a heat index for Hanoi.

Hydration and heat illness

  • WHO: drink enough water throughout the day, bring a refillable bottle and avoid excessive caffeine and alcohol; dark yellow urine may indicate not drinking enough.
  • Smartraveller: drink plenty of water, even if not thirsty, and avoid alcohol.
  • NCHMF bulletin: heat can dehydrate the body after long exposure to high temperatures.
  • WHO: know the signs of heat illness (dizziness, nausea or confusion) and seek medical help if needed. Smartraveller says heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke, which can be fatal if not treated.
  • WHO also lists cooling down with wet towels, misting fans or water splashed on the face and arms.
  • Smartraveller (page updated 18 August 2026): UV radiation can be dangerously high during extreme heat and cause sunburn in as little as 11 minutes.

These are the pages' statements, not medical advice, and the pages give no amounts of water.

Riding and clothing notes from road-safety pages

The UK Highway Code (Department for Transport, updated 22 October 2025) says in rule 237 that the road surface may become soft, or slippery if it rains after a dry spell, which could affect steering and braking; that a driver dazzled by bright sunlight should slow down and, if necessary, stop; and that a vehicle should be kept well ventilated to avoid drowsiness. Ontario's Motorcycle Handbook (updated 31 March 2026) says to wear a jacket and pants that cover the arms and legs completely, even in warm weather, with clothes snug enough not to flap, and not to ride when tired because fatigue affects the ability to perceive and react to emergencies. Both pages are written for other countries and for road use in general, not for Hanoi heat. For wider tips, see Motorbike Riding Safety in Hanoi: Essential Tips, and for an overview of renting in the city, Hanoi Scooter Rental: Complete Guide for Travelers.

Where the sources differ

On clothing, the pages pull in different directions. Smartraveller advises loose, lightweight, light-coloured clothing, and WHO advises breathable, loose-fitting light-colour clothes and a hat. Ontario's handbook asks for full arm and leg cover even in warm weather and clothes snug enough not to flap. The pages do not reconcile these, and none addresses what a rider might wear in Hanoi's heat. The sources also differ in audience: WHO and Smartraveller write for the public and travellers, CDC for outdoor workers, and the Vietnamese pages for forecast users.

What the pages leave out

No page gives a heat index value for Hanoi, a heat-index threshold for riders, or a ride-length limit. None describes riding a scooter in heat in particular, names suitable hours, or says how much water to drink. The Vietnamese outlook is a seasonal estimate from April, and the NCHMF bulletin's year is not shown. The definitions page dates from May 2025 and may have been updated since. No page says anything about rental bikes, helmets supplied, storage, prices or opening hours.

Sources checked

  • Vietnam Hydro-Meteorological Administration: Hanoi heat outlook (7 April 2026)
  • Vietnam Hydro-Meteorological Administration: heat concepts (8 May 2025)
  • NCHMF: heat forecast bulletin
  • CDC NIOSH: heat index bulletin
  • Smartraveller: severe hot or cold weather (18 August 2026)
  • WHO: tips for keeping cool
  • UK Highway Code: adverse weather
  • Ontario handbook: getting ready to drive

Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà is open 09:00–21:00 daily at Ngõ 5 Nguyễn Văn Cừ, Bồ Đề, Long Biên, Hà Nội (near Gia Lâm bus station). Phone: 0334 699 969.
